record.reason: Large language model agents have shown strong promise for clinical decision support over electronic health records (EHR), yet current approaches treat tasks in isolation and lack capacities for self-evolution through accumulated experience. We propose U-EHR, a Unified EHR Agent with Retrospective Memory Evolution that enables continuous capability improvement through closed-loop experiential learning. U-EHR introduces three tightly integrated mechanisms: (1) Step-Level Trajectory Scoring evaluates each action in an execution trajectory along relevance, progress, and correctness dimensions, providing fine-grained credit assignment that distinguishes effective behaviors from detrimental ones within the same trajectory. (2) Dual-Polarity Memory Extraction transforms these quality signals into structured experiential knowledge by distilling both positive patterns worth emulating and negative lessons to avoid. (3) UCB-Guided Memory Retrieval formulates memory selection as a multi-armed bandit problem grounded in the Upper Confidence Bound principle, strategically selecting the most relevant memories from a growing knowledge base while exploring underutilized entries to prevent stagnation. As execution outcomes feed back to refine memory quality estimates and retrieval statistics, the three components form a self-reinforcing evolution cycle that continuously improves the agent's behavioral knowledge without external supervision. Extensive experiments on both the public MIMIC benchmark and our newly introduced Chinese clinical benchmark CN-EHR across diverse clinical tasks demonstrate that U-EHR consistently surpasses existing methods in accuracy and efficiency, with sustained performance gains as experience accumulates, validating the effectiveness of the proposed self-evolution paradigm. Notably, U-EHR exhibits strong cross-lingual generalizability on CN-EHR, suggesting that the learned experiential knowledge transfers across diverse healthcare environments.
record.title: U-EHR: A Self-Evolving EHR Agent with Step-Level Credit Assignment and UCB-Guided Memory Retrieval
